questions.title: Why calibrate for each objective?
opts: The graticule is in the eyepiece, so it looks the same at every objective, while the slide is magnified more or less.
The stage micrometer is in the eyepiece, so its divisions change with the objective, while the graticule stays the same size.
A stronger objective makes the divisions of the graticule shrink, so each one stands for a longer length on the slide.
Each objective lens changes the focus of the eyepiece, so the graticule moves away from its 0 line after every change.

questions.title: A cell at an angle to the scale
opts: Turn the eyepiece until the scale lies along the longest axis, then count the units from one edge to the other.
Count the units straight across the cell as it lies, then add the angle between the cell and the scale to the answer.
Change to the ×10 objective, so that the cell becomes small enough to lie along the scale at any angle you choose.
Measure the cell with a ruler held against the slide, because the scale only works for cells that already lie along it.

questions.title: Magnification and actual size from a scale bar
A scale bar for your own drawing
Actual size in an electron micrograph
A mistake with units
opts: The two lengths are in different units: 25 mm is 25 000 µm, so the magnification is 25 000 ÷ 10 = ×2500.
The division is the wrong way round: magnification = 10 ÷ 25 = ×0.4, because the scale bar is the smaller length.
Nothing went wrong: a magnification is always the length of the scale bar divided by the number written beside it.
The scale bar must be measured in centimetres, so the magnification is 2.5 ÷ 10 = ×0.25, which is smaller again.

questions.title: Recall the rules for a drawing
A photo with no scale in it
opts: Your measurement of the cell’s size, because nothing in the photo shows the scale you used.
Your choice of cell, because a photo cannot show which of the cells on the slide you chose to draw.
Your staining, because the colour of a stain always changes when a phone takes a photo of it.
The labels of your drawing, because the structures in a photo have no names written beside them.
